part_title: Human Labeling, Active Learning and Ground Truth Plus

scenes.title: Human Labeling Workflow
scenes.narration: Let's zoom in on a single label task. An S3 bucket contains unlabeled inputs. The next panel specifies the task and instructions—for example, examine an image and choose the correct animal category. Human annotators open a labeling interface, inspect the image and select a label. Then a quality-review stage checks the submission, including whether the label matches the image and instructions. Finally, approved label outputs and a manifest are written to a destination in S3. Notice the different roles in the diagram: task authors define instructions, workers label examples, and reviewers assess accuracy. If the task definition is ambiguous, adding more workers won't fix the underlying problem. A useful labeling job therefore needs unambiguous examples, quality thresholds and a plan for disagreements. The labeled dataset is only as trustworthy as the process that produced it.

scenes.title: Active Learning for Labels
scenes.narration: This slide illustrates an active-learning strategy. Unlabeled records enter a model that predicts labels and associated confidence. Follow the upper cyan path: highly confident predictions can be candidates for automated labeling, subject to validation and supported workflow rules. The lower orange path collects low-confidence or ambiguous examples for human annotators. After review, those examples become part of an improved training set. The loop returns to the model so it can learn from the hard cases. This arrangement focuses expensive human effort where it can add the most value. But confidence is not guaranteed correctness, particularly when the input distribution changes or the model is poorly calibrated. Include random quality checks and diverse samples so errors in the high-confidence branch do not silently become training truth. Active learning is a sampling and review strategy, not an excuse to skip validation.

scenes.title: Choose a Labeling Workforce
scenes.narration: The comparison has three columns: a private workforce, a managed vendor workforce, and a public workforce where supported. A private workforce uses employees or trusted contractors and can provide stronger control over sensitive data and domain expertise. A vendor workforce offers outsourced capacity and process management, depending on the arrangement. A public workforce may scale common labeling tasks but is less appropriate for confidential or specialist datasets. Look at the table at the bottom comparing control, expertise and scale. The choice depends on privacy, required skills, cost and volume, not just how many people can annotate quickly. For a healthcare or security dataset, access controls and specialist review may dominate the decision. For a simple public-image classification task, a broader workforce may be viable. Set consistent instructions and quality checks regardless of the workforce.

scenes.title: Ground Truth Plus
scenes.narration: Ground Truth Plus is depicted as a managed labeling program rather than only a labeling UI. The four steps run from left to right. First, define the task, label taxonomy, quality targets and instructions. Second, submit input data from S3. Third, review job progress and quality indicators while the managed team performs supported labeling work. Fourth, receive the completed labeled output in an S3 bucket. The orange title emphasizes human expertise and a fully managed program. For an organization without its own large annotation operation, this can reduce workforce-management effort. It still requires the organization to define success criteria, provide appropriate sample data and examine delivered quality. An output file appearing in S3 does not automatically guarantee that every edge case was understood. Plan evaluation samples, a process for disputes and suitable privacy protection before beginning a large labeling project.

scenes.title: Machine-Assisted Labeling with Review
scenes.narration: This slide shows a hybrid labeling pipeline. First, a supported machine-learning service such as Amazon Rekognition or Comprehend suggests labels for data—for example, an animal category or sentiment. Next, human reviewers inspect those suggestions in a labeling workflow. Third, reviewers correct mistakes, refine labels and resolve ambiguous examples. Finally, the system exports the validated labels and manifests for training or evaluation. Notice the two benefits along the bottom: automation reduces repetitive work, while human review improves precision and consistency. The example dog image illustrates why a suggested label needs confirmation if the task's taxonomy is more specific than the model predicts. Machine-generated labels can inherit bias or domain mismatch, so validation samples remain necessary. Use the hybrid approach when suggested labels save time without reducing the quality the downstream model requires.
